chapter_theme: The prince tames an elephant and a horse and masters learning; his stepmother-like rival's talk leads the king to order him away, and the prince answers by a show of riding, by winning at dice from kings and giving it back, so that the king builds him his own city of Alankarapuram.

cast.role: the hero, son of Jayandhara and Prithivi-devi
the king of Rajamagriha, the prince's father (named in line 4 of verse 62)
a queen of the king (Visalakanni, Visalanetrai), who speaks of the prince's fame and is taken as accuser
Visalanetri's son, who plots after hearing of the prince's fame
the prince's mother, who tells him what has happened
the king's servants who report and carry out the seizure
the neighbouring kings who play dice with the prince

57.reading: The prince goes after a maddened elephant that has been wrecking the city's mansions, subdues it, lets it go to the king, and the king bids his other son keep it.
57.nuance: The rut that the prince masters is the same maddened state (மதம்) that the sage's prophecy in verse 46 had named, so the feat reads as the fulfilment of a foretold sign. Line 3 and 4 do not make clear which son the king addresses (வாகுநற் சுதன்): the reading follows the word order.
57.event: Naga Kumaran subdues the elephant that has run amok in the city and offers it to the king, who tells his son to take it.

58.reading: On another day the prince masters a vicious horse, rides it through every street with a fire-brand and shows it to the victorious king, who tells him to keep it; he takes it home.
58.nuance: Line 2 (தீக்கோடி ஆட்டி) is not clear; it is read here as a flourish with fire while riding.
58.event: Naga Kumaran tames a vicious horse, parades it through the streets and presents it to the king, who lets him keep it.

59.reading: Having gained the four things the sage's teaching of dharma had pointed to, the prince crosses the sea of learning, rides elephants and chariot horses with renown, and grows like the waxing moon into a distinguished youth.
59.nuance: The 'four' (நான்கு) are not named in the verse; they are taken as the four things the sage foretold or set out in the earlier teaching. The verse ties worldly mastery to the sage's words and not to the prince's own effort alone.
59.event: Naga Kumaran grows up, masters the arts and the riding of elephants and horses, and comes of age.

claims.claim: a prince who follows the sage's teaching of dharma gains the four ends and mastery of learning

60.reading: Visalakanni, seeing her son, tells him kindly that she has heard the prince's fame spread beyond telling through all the lands, that she has no great merit, and that he should so act that no blame touches him and he be protected.
60.nuance: Line 3 (பெருந்தவம் இல்லை நீயும்) can be read as the speaker's own lack of merit or a charge that her son lacks it; the speaker's tone, kindly or envious, is not fixed. The son (சுதன்) is taken as Srithara, because verse 61 turns to him.
60.event: Visalanetri speaks to her son Srithara of Naga Kumaran's spreading fame.

61.reading: Srithara, hearing this, resolves in his heart what to do, and gathers five hundred men of skilled hands, one of whom is to be the killer of a thousand, and stays on happily until the day comes.
61.nuance: The lines on the thousand and five hundred are obscure; whether the men are assassins or a guard is not settled by the verse itself, and the plot is a reading from the next verses.
61.event: Srithara plans against Naga Kumaran and assembles five hundred skilled men.

62.reading: The prince and his fair wives bathe in the pond called Kuccam while a maid carries garlands, saffron and silk; meanwhile Jayandhara sits on the upper floor of his mansion.
62.event: Naga Kumaran bathes in the pond with his wives while the king watches from the upper floor.

63.reading: The king's queen Visalanetri comes to the pond's bank and stands there, and the prince bows to her on seeing her.
63.nuance: Line 2 speaks of a thief who couples with another's wife; it suggests a charge laid against the prince but the syntax is broken, so the accusation is only inferred from verses 64 and 65.
63.event: Visalanetri comes to the pond's bank where Naga Kumaran sees her and bows.

64.reading: The king rages at the woman who has spun falsehood, while the prince and his slender wife, adorned with garlands and sandal, go back with the attendant to their great house.
64.nuance: The verse says plainly that a lie was fabricated (பொய்யுரை புனைந்தவளை) but not who is accused or who lies; the king's anger may fall on the liar or on the person she slandered.
64.event: The king is enraged at the woman's lie; the prince and his wife return to their house.

65.reading: The king asks his queen where she had gone, why she went to watch her son bathe, why he plays with her in the house, and tells that he must go and play outside the city.
65.nuance: The addressee (தேவி) and whose son is meant are not clear; the verse is read as the king sending Naga Kumaran to live outside the capital, which verse 73 then carries out.
65.event: Jayandhara questions the queen and orders the prince out of the city to play.

66.reading: The king leaves after speaking; the queen bows her head, joyless and grieving; the prince, clever, comes in wonder and asks her, and on hearing the king's word he mounts an elephant.
66.event: The queen grieves at the king's order; Naga Kumaran asks her, hears of the order and mounts an elephant.

67.reading: With drums sounding, the prince subdues a rutting elephant and displays circling riding in every street to the sound of many instruments, and the king hears of the angry procession.
67.nuance: The prince's riding is a show of his mastery in the face of the order to leave; the verse does not say he is defying it, but the king takes it as such in verse 68.
67.event: Naga Kumaran parades on a rutting elephant through the streets and the king hears of it.

68.reading: Servants tell the king that the prince has overstepped his sweet word; the king bids them enter his house and take the golden ornaments and goods, and they seize them.
68.nuance: The verse gives no sign that the story judges the stripping unjust or just; it reports the king's order as an act of sceptre, and verses 69 to 72 show the prince turning it round by dice.
68.event: The king, told that the prince disobeyed, orders his house stripped of ornaments and goods, and the servants take them.

69.reading: The prince comes down from his elephant, his mother tells him what has happened, and he goes into the house to play at dice, beats the kings, and takes away the ornaments that gather.
69.nuance: The text of line 4 ends in a stray punctuation mark; the order of events is hard to fix.
69.event: On his mother's telling Naga Kumaran plays dice with the kings, beats them and carries off their ornaments.

70.reading: All the kings, at the great king's sight, bow, with serpent-gem necklaces, pearl garlands, bracelets and armlets, and a cry goes up about the matter.
70.nuance: Line 4 (வேந்தென்ன இக்கூற்றென) is corrupt or obscure; the sense is a guess.
70.event: The kings bow before the king with their jewels gathered.

71.reading: A speaker tells the king that by dice he has won the prince's ornaments, that the prince invited him to play and then, out of love for his father, beat him greatly in two games.
71.nuance: The speaker is not named; he is read as one of the kings who played, but the verse could also be the king's own account.
71.event: A king reports to Jayandhara that he won the prince's jewels at dice and then lost twice to him.

72.reading: The prince gives each king who had agreed to play the hereditary goods that rightly belong to them, returns home and hands the rest to his mother, and gives the kings their own necklaces back.
72.nuance: The dice are the means by which a prince put out of his goods wins goods back, and the story ends not in keeping them but in giving them away, which the Kural's warning on gambling does not allow for.
72.event: Naga Kumaran returns the kings' hereditary property and necklaces, and gives the rest to his mother.

73.reading: By the king's command a fine city is built outside the great city for the prince to live in, and it is called Alankarapuram; the youth wears a gold garland there.
73.event: Jayandhara orders a city built outside the capital where Naga Kumaran lives, named Alankarapuram.

links.note: The sage had foretold that the prince would curb the rut of a great elephant; verse 57 shows him doing so on the city's own mad elephant.
links.teaches: The sage's prophecy is not left as a promise: the city's real elephant is the first thing that proves it, so a reader sees the prince's prowess as the working of what was foretold.

links.note: The sage's dream-reading promised a son who would bear great austerity and cut off karma; verse 59 shows him grown in learning by the sage's teaching, the first step toward that end.
links.teaches: The prophecy of renunciation is paired here with a worldly rise, so the story shows the prince's skill as a stage on the way to release and not a rival to it.

links.note: The king's order to play outside the city becomes, in verse 73, his command to build the prince a city of his own and name it.
links.teaches: The expulsion is turned into an honour by the end of the chapter, so the sentence of exile never takes effect as a punishment.

links.note: The king had ordered the prince's goods taken; in 72 the prince, enriched by dice, gives away all that he wins to the kings and his mother.
links.teaches: The order to strip the prince is answered not by revenge but by the prince's giving, so the seizure leaves him richer in standing than the king who ordered it.

links.note: Kovalan frees a Brahmin from a rogue elephant and tames it, and Naga Kumaran subdues a maddened elephant that has been wrecking the city: the same feat of a hero.
links.teaches: In the Silappathikaram the feat is an act of compassion for one man; in this epic it is a sign of a foretold destiny and a cause of royal suspicion.

links.note: The prince masters a rutting elephant; Tirumular's body holds five rutting elephants that will not come to the post of the Agamas' teaching.
links.teaches: The epic's taming is an outward feat of the body, and the Tirumanthiram carries the same image inward to the senses, so the story's word மதம் is read both as rut and as the pride the senses breed.

gains.a: The epic's elephant gains a second sense: its mastery is also a figure for the senses held in check.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram's inner elephants gain a narrative picture, a man who actually stops a rampaging beast.

links.note: The prince mounts and rides a vicious horse through the streets; Tirumular tells the reader to hold the reins of the running horse firmly.
links.teaches: The ride of a hero is shown in the epic as skill before a crowd, and in the Tirumanthiram as the discipline of the mind that needs no show, so the two use one image for different ends.

gains.a: The prince's horse-taming gains a reading as the discipline of a restless will.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram's running horse gains a visible rider and a crowd, a show that the verse tells its hearers to do without.

links.note: The prince wins at dice from the kings, as the Kural warns that what a gambler wins is like the hook's metal in the fish.
links.teaches: The Kural treats winning as the lure; the epic gives a winner who is not caught by it because he gives the winnings back, which shows the rule is about the winner's grip on the goods.

gains.a: The prince's win gains a measure: it is the keeping of the winnings, not the playing, that the couplet condemns.
gains.b: The couplet's warning gains a hard case, a winner who takes nothing, which tests whether the warning is about the game or the hunger.

links.note: The prince is accused through a lie told against him and keeps his bearing; the Naladiyar says the pure of heart are not shaken by cruel slander, like a lamp's flame.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar's steadiness under slander is shown in the epic as a prince who answers the false charge with a procession and with giving, not with protest.

gains.a: The verse gains a character who passes the Naladiyar's test of staying unshaken by false speech.
gains.b: The Naladiyar quatrain gains a story in which the slander is followed by exile and a city, so the cost and the outcome of steadiness are shown.

source_issues: Verses 60 to 71 are hard to read: the text names no accuser or accusation, and several lines (60.3, 61.2-3, 63.2, 64.1, 69.2, 70.4) are corrupt or obscure.
Verse 69 ends with a stray full stop and semicolon.
Chapter 4 opens in the middle of a scene; verse 57 is the end of the elephant episode begun in the previous chapter's prophecy.
